igcse-0580-fdp-fraction-forms.description: Read, simplify and convert proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers for Cambridge IGCSE 0580.

sections.title: What do the top and bottom numbers tell you?
sections.label: Read a fraction
sections.intro: A fraction counts equal parts of a whole. Use the same-sized whole throughout a comparison.

blocks.html: In \(\frac{4}{9}\), the denominator \(9\) gives the number of parts in one whole and the numerator \(4\) gives the number counted.
Reading the fraction as nine parts out of four swaps the two roles.

blocks.title: Read the named fraction form
blocks.prompt: Which form is \(\frac{15}{8}\) written in?

retry.feedback: It is a single fraction, with no separate whole-number part.

blocks.hint: A mixed number has a separate whole-number part printed beside the fraction.
blocks.solution:
The numerator is \(15\) and the denominator is \(8\).

The numerator is greater than the denominator, so it is a improper fraction.

blocks.html: Look for the dividing line when identifying numerator and denominator.

sections.title: How can two fractions show the same amount?
sections.label: Make an equivalent fraction
sections.intro: If each equal part is split into two, both the count of parts and the count in one whole double.

blocks.html: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same positive whole number. The value is unchanged.

figure.alt: Two equal-length strips show three shaded sections out of five above six shaded sections out of ten. Their shaded lengths end at the same position.
figure.caption: Both strips show the same amount. \(\frac35=\frac6{10}\) because splitting every fifth in two doubles both counts.

blocks.html: Multiplying just one number changes the fraction.

blocks.title: Scale both parts of the fraction
blocks.prompt: Find the missing numerator in \(\frac{5}{13}=\frac{n}{52}\).

retry.feedback: The denominator was scaled. The numerator needs the same multiplier.

blocks.hint: Compare the denominators first, then apply their scale factor to the top.
blocks.solution:
The denominator is multiplied by \(4\). To keep the same value, multiply the numerator by that same number.

\(n=5\times4=20\).

blocks.html: Find the scale factor from the number you know in both fractions.

sections.title: When has a fraction been simplified completely?
sections.label: Use smallest terms
sections.intro: An equivalent fraction can use smaller integers without changing the measured amount.

blocks.html: Divide both numbers by a common factor. Once their highest common factor is \(1\), the fraction is in simplest form.
Subtracting the same number from top and bottom does not simplify a fraction.

blocks.title: Write the fraction in lowest terms
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{45}{70}\) in simplest form. Give the numerator and the denominator.

retry.feedback: Simplest form keeps the value but uses the smallest positive denominator. Divide the top and bottom by their common factor.

blocks.hint: Find a number greater than 1 that divides both numbers.
blocks.solution:
A common factor of both numbers is \(5\). Divide both by that factor.

\(\frac{45}{70}=\frac{45\div5}{70\div5}=\frac{9}{14}\).

The resulting numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than \(1\).

blocks.html: Using the highest common factor gets to simplest form in one step.

sections.title: Why can a mixed number be written as one fraction?
sections.label: Mixed to improper
sections.intro: The whole number and the fraction use the same unit of measurement.

blocks.html: Multiply the whole part by the denominator to count the parts in those wholes. Add the original numerator and keep the denominator.

figure.alt: Two equal rectangles are fully filled. A third equal rectangle is split into fourths with its first three parts filled.
figure.caption: The three bars show \(2\tfrac{3}{4}\). Counting quarters instead gives \(\frac{11}{4}\).

blocks.html: Adding the whole number directly to the numerator counts whole units as though they were single parts.

blocks.title: Count the parts in the whole numbers
blocks.prompt: Write \(3\tfrac{4}{9}\) as an improper fraction. Give its numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The whole part contains several groups of the denominator. Count those parts before adding the numerator.

blocks.hint: Think of the whole numbers as repeated groups the same size as the denominator.
blocks.solution:
Each whole contains \(9\) parts of this size. So \(3\) wholes contain \(3\times9=27\) parts.

Include the \(4\) extra parts to obtain \(31\) parts of size \(\frac{1}{9}\).

The resulting improper fraction is \(\frac{31}{9}\).

blocks.html: Check the result is greater than the original whole part.

sections.title: How does division turn an improper fraction into a mixed number?
sections.label: Improper to mixed
sections.intro: Group the parts into complete wholes. What remains is the fraction after the whole part.

blocks.html: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The quotient is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator initially stays the same.
The remainder must be smaller than the denominator. If the remainder is zero, the result is a whole number.

blocks.title: Find the whole groups and the remainder
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{53}{12}\) as a mixed number in simplest form. Give its whole part, numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The fraction numerator is the remainder, after removing all the complete wholes.

blocks.hint: Count how many complete groups of the denominator fit into the numerator.
blocks.solution:
\(53=4\times12+5\). This counts \(4\) complete wholes and \(5\) parts left over.

The remaining fraction is \(\frac{5}{12}\) because each original whole was split into \(12\) equal parts.

The mixed number is \(4\tfrac{5}{12}\).

blocks.html: Simplify the remaining fraction if its numerator and denominator still share a factor.

examples.title: Read the named fraction form
examples.question: Which form is \(\frac{4}{9}\) written in?
solution: The numerator is \(4\) and the denominator is \(9\).
The numerator is less than the denominator, so it is a proper fraction.

examples.title: Read the named fraction form
examples.question: Which form is \(\frac{13}{6}\) written in?
solution: The numerator is \(13\) and the denominator is \(6\).
The numerator is greater than the denominator, so it is a improper fraction.

examples.title: Scale both parts of the fraction
examples.question: Find the missing numerator in \(\frac{7}{12}=\frac{n}{36}\).
solution: The denominator is multiplied by \(3\). To keep the same value, multiply the numerator by that same number.

examples.title: Write the fraction in lowest terms
examples.question: Write \(\frac{30}{48}\) in simplest form. Give the numerator and the denominator.
solution: A common factor of both numbers is \(6\). Divide both by that factor.
The resulting numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than \(1\).

examples.title: Write the fraction in lowest terms
examples.question: Write \(\frac{28}{44}\) in simplest form. Give the numerator and the denominator.
solution: A common factor of both numbers is \(4\). Divide both by that factor.
The resulting numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than \(1\).

examples.title: Count the parts in the whole numbers
examples.question: Write \(4\tfrac{5}{8}\) as an improper fraction. Give its numerator and denominator.
solution: Each whole contains \(8\) parts of this size. So \(4\) wholes contain \(4\times8=32\) parts.
Include the \(5\) extra parts to obtain \(37\) parts of size \(\frac{1}{8}\).
The resulting improper fraction is \(\frac{37}{8}\).

examples.title: Find the whole groups and the remainder
examples.question: Write \(\frac{37}{7}\) as a mixed number in simplest form. Give its whole part, numerator and denominator.
solution: \(37=5\times7+2\). This counts \(5\) complete wholes and \(2\) parts left over.
The remaining fraction is \(\frac{2}{7}\) because each original whole was split into \(7\) equal parts.
The mixed number is \(5\tfrac{2}{7}\).

glossary.definition: The number of equal parts being counted.
The number of equal parts in one whole.
A positive fraction whose numerator is smaller than its denominator.
A fraction with a numerator at least as large as its positive denominator.
A whole number written with an additional proper fraction.

extraPractice.title: Scale both parts of the fraction
extraPractice.prompt: Find the missing numerator in \(\frac{8}{15}=\frac{n}{90}\).

retry.feedback: The denominator was scaled. The numerator needs the same multiplier.

extraPractice.hint: Compare the denominators first, then apply their scale factor to the top.
extraPractice.solution:
The denominator is multiplied by \(6\). To keep the same value, multiply the numerator by that same number.

\(n=8\times6=48\).

extraPractice.title: Write the fraction in lowest terms
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{44}{68}\) in simplest form. Give the numerator and the denominator.

retry.feedback: Simplest form keeps the value but uses the smallest positive denominator. Divide the top and bottom by their common factor.

extraPractice.hint: Find a number greater than 1 that divides both numbers.
extraPractice.solution:
A common factor of both numbers is \(4\). Divide both by that factor.

\(\frac{44}{68}=\frac{44\div4}{68\div4}=\frac{11}{17}\).

The resulting numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than \(1\).

extraPractice.title: Count the parts in the whole numbers
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(6\tfrac{3}{7}\) as an improper fraction. Give its numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The whole part contains several groups of the denominator. Count those parts before adding the numerator.

extraPractice.hint: Think of the whole numbers as repeated groups the same size as the denominator.
extraPractice.solution:
Each whole contains \(7\) parts of this size. So \(6\) wholes contain \(6\times7=42\) parts.

Include the \(3\) extra parts to obtain \(45\) parts of size \(\frac{1}{7}\).

The resulting improper fraction is \(\frac{45}{7}\).

extraPractice.title: Find the whole groups and the remainder
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{37}{10}\) as a mixed number in simplest form. Give its whole part, numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The fraction numerator is the remainder, after removing all the complete wholes.

extraPractice.hint: Count how many complete groups of the denominator fit into the numerator.
extraPractice.solution:
\(37=3\times10+7\). This counts \(3\) complete wholes and \(7\) parts left over.

The remaining fraction is \(\frac{7}{10}\) because each original whole was split into \(10\) equal parts.

The mixed number is \(3\tfrac{7}{10}\).

extraPractice.title: Write the fraction in lowest terms
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{35}{84}\) in simplest form. Give the numerator and the denominator.

retry.feedback: Simplest form keeps the value but uses the smallest positive denominator. Divide the top and bottom by their common factor.

extraPractice.hint: Find a number greater than 1 that divides both numbers.
extraPractice.solution:
A common factor of both numbers is \(7\). Divide both by that factor.

\(\frac{35}{84}=\frac{35\div7}{84\div7}=\frac{5}{12}\).

The resulting numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than \(1\).

extraPractice.title: Find the whole groups and the remainder
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{92}{11}\) as a mixed number in simplest form. Give its whole part, numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The fraction numerator is the remainder, after removing all the complete wholes.

extraPractice.hint: Count how many complete groups of the denominator fit into the numerator.
extraPractice.solution:
\(92=8\times11+4\). This counts \(8\) complete wholes and \(4\) parts left over.

The remaining fraction is \(\frac{4}{11}\) because each original whole was split into \(11\) equal parts.

The mixed number is \(8\tfrac{4}{11}\).

revision.body:
Conversion methods

Starting pointWhat to do
Name the formA proper fraction is less than one. A mixed number has a separate whole part.
Make an equivalent fractionMultiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.
Mixed → improper\(w\,\tfrac ab=\frac{wb+a}{b}\)
Improper → mixedDivide for the whole part. Put the remainder over the original denominator.
revision.checks:
• Keep the unit size fixed.
  • The remainder must be smaller than the denominator.
  • Check both parts for a common factor.
revision.examTip: Rebuild the original numerator from the whole part and the remainder to verify your answer.

igcse-0580-fdp-terminating-decimals.description: Use place value and exact division to convert terminating decimals and fractions in Cambridge IGCSE 0580.

sections.title: How does a decimal tell you the size of the parts?
sections.label: Read place value
sections.intro: After the decimal point, each place is one tenth of the place to its left.

blocks.html: A value with three decimal places can be read as a whole number of thousandths. Write leading or internal zero digits in their original places.

figure.alt: A square is divided into ten rows of ten cells. Four full rows and six cells of the next row are shaded.
figure.caption: Every shaded square is one hundredth. Forty-six squares show \(\frac{46}{100}=0.46\).

blocks.html: The digit in the thousandths position is just one digit. The complete number may contain many thousandths.

blocks.title: Locate hundredths and thousandths separately
blocks.prompt: For \(0.524\), give the digit in the hundredths column and the number of thousandths in the whole value.
blocks.hint: The digit in the thousandths column is different from the number of thousandths in the complete number.
blocks.solution:
To the right of the decimal point the place values are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

The hundredths digit is \(2\). As the whole value is \(\frac{524}{1000}\), it contains \(524\) thousandths.

blocks.html: Track the units, tenths, hundredths and thousandths positions in order.

sections.title: How do you write a terminating decimal as a fraction?
sections.label: Use a power of ten
sections.intro: The last position gives the initial denominator.

blocks.html: For \(d\) decimal places, write the digits over \(10^d\) and then simplify.
Writing a decimal with three decimal places over \(100\) gives a value ten times too large.

blocks.title: Use the last decimal place
blocks.prompt: Write \(0.266\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The power of ten is a starting denominator. Simplify the fraction before entering its final denominator.

blocks.hint: Count every place after the decimal point, including zeros.
blocks.solution:
There are \(3\) places after the decimal point. Read the number as \(\frac{266}{1000}\) using place value.

Divide both parts by their highest common factor, \(2\).

This gives \(\frac{133}{500}\).

blocks.html: Treat trailing zeros as extra places if you count them. Simplifying gives the same final fraction.

sections.title: Can you change the fraction to tenths or hundredths first?
sections.label: Scale to a power of ten
sections.intro: Equivalent fractions give a direct route from several common denominators.

blocks.html: Choose \(10\), \(100\) or another suitable power of ten divisible by the denominator. Scale top and bottom equally.
A denominator that looks close to 100 cannot simply be rounded or changed on its own.

blocks.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{9}{125}\) as an exact terminating decimal.

retry.feedback: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Reversing that order gives the reciprocal.

blocks.hint: Use the top number as the dividend.
blocks.solution:
Use a denominator of \(1000\). Multiply the top and bottom by \(8\).

\(\frac{9}{125}=\frac{72}{1000}=0.072\).

blocks.html: When a fraction is already over \(1000\), read the decimal directly.

sections.title: When is division the better route?
sections.label: Divide top by bottom
sections.intro: The fraction bar also means division. This works for improper fractions as well.

blocks.html: Put the numerator into the division and use the denominator as the divisor. Start with the whole part if the numerator is larger.
Dividing the denominator by the numerator calculates the reciprocal and usually gives a different magnitude.

blocks.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
blocks.prompt: Write \(\frac{39}{48}\) as an exact terminating decimal.

retry.feedback: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Reversing that order gives the reciprocal.

blocks.hint: Use the top number as the dividend.
blocks.solution:
First simplify \(\frac{39}{48}\) to \(\frac{13}{16}\).

Divide the numerator by the denominator. This gives the exact decimal \(0.8125\).

blocks.html: For a proper fraction, the decimal result is below one.

sections.title: How can you check that the forms are exactly equal?
sections.label: Verify a conversion
sections.intro: Recognise the same number after changing the representation.

blocks.html: Convert the decimal back to a fraction, or multiply it by the original denominator to recover the original numerator.
A decimal that is only rounded to a few places is not an exact equivalent.

blocks.title: Spot the matching terminating decimal
blocks.prompt: Which decimal equals \(\frac{21}{80}\) exactly?
blocks.hint: Estimate whether the fraction is below or above one first.
blocks.solution:
Convert \(\frac{21}{80}\) by dividing. The exact decimal is \(0.2625\).

You can check it by multiplying that decimal by the denominator to recover the numerator.

blocks.html: If the forms are equal, checking in either direction should return the same value.

examples.title: Locate hundredths and thousandths separately
examples.question: For \(0.378\), give the digit in the hundredths column and the number of thousandths in the whole value.
solution: To the right of the decimal point the place values are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
The hundredths digit is \(7\). As the whole value is \(\frac{378}{1000}\), it contains \(378\) thousandths.

examples.title: Locate hundredths and thousandths separately
examples.question: For \(0.049\), give the digit in the hundredths column and the number of thousandths in the whole value.
solution: To the right of the decimal point the place values are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
The hundredths digit is \(4\). As the whole value is \(\frac{49}{1000}\), it contains \(49\) thousandths.

examples.title: Use the last decimal place
examples.question: Write \(1.236\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
solution: There are \(3\) places after the decimal point. Read the number as \(\frac{1236}{1000}\) using place value.
Divide both parts by their highest common factor, \(4\).
This gives \(\frac{309}{250}\).

examples.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
examples.question: Write \(\frac{11}{25}\) as an exact terminating decimal.
solution: Use a denominator of \(100\). Multiply the top and bottom by \(4\).

examples.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
examples.question: Write \(\frac{27}{40}\) as an exact terminating decimal.
solution: Use a denominator of \(1000\). Multiply the top and bottom by \(25\).

examples.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
examples.question: Write \(\frac{21}{48}\) as an exact terminating decimal.
solution: First simplify \(\frac{21}{48}\) to \(\frac{7}{16}\).
Divide the numerator by the denominator. This gives the exact decimal \(0.4375\).

examples.title: Spot the matching terminating decimal
examples.question: Which decimal equals \(\frac{19}{32}\) exactly?
solution: Convert \(\frac{19}{32}\) by dividing. The exact decimal is \(0.59375\).
You can check it by multiplying that decimal by the denominator to recover the numerator.

glossary.definition: The value attached to a digit because of its position.
An exact decimal with finitely many digits after the decimal point.

extraPractice.title: Use the last decimal place
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(2.073\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
extraPractice.hint: Count every place after the decimal point, including zeros.
extraPractice.solution:
There are \(3\) places after the decimal point. Read the number as \(\frac{2073}{1000}\) using place value.

Divide both parts by their highest common factor, \(1\).

This gives \(\frac{2073}{1000}\).

extraPractice.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{23}{50}\) as an exact terminating decimal.

retry.feedback: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Reversing that order gives the reciprocal.

extraPractice.hint: Use the top number as the dividend.
extraPractice.solution:
Use a denominator of \(100\). Multiply the top and bottom by \(2\).

\(\frac{23}{50}=\frac{46}{100}=0.46\).

extraPractice.title: Convert the fraction to an exact decimal
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(\frac{36}{96}\) as an exact terminating decimal.

retry.feedback: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Reversing that order gives the reciprocal.

extraPractice.hint: Use the top number as the dividend.
extraPractice.solution:
First simplify \(\frac{36}{96}\) to \(\frac{3}{8}\).

Divide the numerator by the denominator. This gives the exact decimal \(0.375\).

extraPractice.title: Use the last decimal place
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(0.0350\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.

retry.feedback: The power of ten is a starting denominator. Simplify the fraction before entering its final denominator.

extraPractice.hint: Count every place after the decimal point, including zeros.
extraPractice.solution:
There are \(4\) places after the decimal point. Read the number as \(\frac{350}{10000}\) using place value.

Divide both parts by their highest common factor, \(50\).

This gives \(\frac{7}{200}\).

extraPractice.title: Spot the matching terminating decimal
extraPractice.prompt: Which decimal equals \(\frac{11}{16}\) exactly?
extraPractice.hint: Estimate whether the fraction is below or above one first.
extraPractice.solution:
Convert \(\frac{11}{16}\) by dividing. The exact decimal is \(0.6875\).

You can check it by multiplying that decimal by the denominator to recover the numerator.

extraPractice.title: Locate hundredths and thousandths separately
extraPractice.prompt: For \(0.706\), give the digit in the hundredths column and the number of thousandths in the whole value.
extraPractice.hint: The digit in the thousandths column is different from the number of thousandths in the complete number.
extraPractice.solution:
To the right of the decimal point the place values are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

The hundredths digit is \(0\). As the whole value is \(\frac{706}{1000}\), it contains \(706\) thousandths.

revision.body:
Conversion methods

Starting pointWhat to do
Read placesTenths, hundredths, thousandths.
Decimal → fraction\(d\) places means a starting denominator \(10^d\). Simplify.
Fraction → decimalScale to an exact power-of-ten denominator or divide top by bottom.
Reverse checkThe decimal times the denominator equals the numerator.
revision.checks:
• Count placeholders after the decimal point.
  • Keep exact digits.
  • Check whether the value is below or above one.
revision.examTip: For a decimal-to-fraction conversion, give the simplest fraction if the question asks for it.

igcse-0580-fdp-percentages.description: Recognise equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages, including fractional percentages and values above one whole.

sections.title: What does the percent sign mean?
sections.label: Per hundred
sections.intro: A percentage is another name for an amount measured against one hundred.

blocks.html: \(p\%=\frac p{100}\). One full unit is \(100\%\).

figure.alt: The first grid has all one hundred squares shaded. The second grid has thirteen squares shaded.
figure.caption: Together the two grids show \(\frac{113}{100}=1.13=113\%\). One whole is \(100\%\).

blocks.html: A percentage number can be greater than 100. It then describes more than one whole.

blocks.title: Give the same value as a percentage
blocks.prompt: Convert \(\frac{41}{50}\). Give the percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.

retry.feedback: This is the decimal value. Give the number obtained after multiplying it by 100.

blocks.hint: The fraction itself is the starting decimal value. Multiply that value by 100 for the percentage.
blocks.solution:
Divide the numerator by the denominator to give \(0.82\).

Multiply that decimal by \(100\). The fraction equals \(82\%\).

blocks.html: Use one whole as a reference before substituting a number.

sections.title: Why multiply the decimal by one hundred?
sections.label: Decimal to percentage
sections.intro: A decimal expresses the value as a number of whole units. The percentage expresses the same value as a number of hundredths.

blocks.html: Multiply by \(100\) to get the percentage number, then attach the percent sign.
A decimal below \(0.01\) gives a percentage below \(1\%\), not a two-digit percentage.

blocks.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
blocks.prompt: Write \(0.098\) as a percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.

retry.feedback: The field asks for the percentage number. Multiply the decimal by 100.

blocks.hint: Anchor the conversion with 1 = 100 per cent.
blocks.solution:
One whole is \(100\%\). Multiply the decimal value by \(100\).

\(0.098\times100=9.8\) gives \(9.8\%\).

blocks.html: Check both directions with \(0.01=1\%\).

sections.title: What happens with a fractional percentage?
sections.label: Percentage to decimal
sections.intro: A given percentage number may itself have decimal places.

blocks.html: Divide the percentage number by \(100\) even when it is less than one or greater than one hundred.
Dropping the percent sign without dividing changes the value by a factor of 100.

blocks.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
blocks.prompt: Write \(3.4\%\) as an exact decimal.

retry.feedback: Percent means per hundred. Divide the given percentage number by 100.

blocks.hint: Anchor the conversion with 1 = 100 per cent.
blocks.solution:
Percent means per hundred. First write the value as \(\frac{3.4}{100}\).

Dividing by \(100\) gives \(0.034\).

blocks.html: For more than one whole the final decimal must be greater than 1.

sections.title: How do you express a percentage as a fraction?
sections.label: Percentage to fraction
sections.intro: Start by interpreting the percent sign as a denominator of 100.

blocks.html: If the number on top has a decimal part, scale numerator and denominator together until they are integers. Then simplify.
Writing a decimal over 100 is a useful intermediate step. A final ordinary fraction has integer numerator and denominator.

blocks.title: Use a fraction with denominator one hundred
blocks.prompt: Write \(64\%\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
blocks.hint: The percent sign becomes “over 100” before you work with the fraction.
blocks.solution:
The percent sign means per hundred, giving \(\frac{64}{100}\).

Remove the decimal in the numerator, if present, by scaling both parts by the same power of ten. Then simplify to \(\frac{16}{25}\).

blocks.html: Check the reduced answer and the percentage are on the same side of one whole.

sections.title: What shows that three forms are equivalent?
sections.label: Match all forms
sections.intro: Each form must name the same number.

blocks.html: Convert to one common reference value. For a terminating fraction, first divide or use an equivalent power-of-ten denominator.
A pair with the correct decimal and an incorrect percentage is an incorrect match.

blocks.title: Match the fraction, decimal and percentage
blocks.prompt: Which pair gives the same value as \(\frac{31}{40}\) in both columns?
blocks.hint: The correct pair must match the fraction in both entries.
blocks.solution:
Write \(\frac{31}{40}\) as \(0.775\).

Its percentage number is \(0.775\times100=77.5\), so select \(0.775\), \(77.5\%\).

blocks.html: Use the % symbol in a written answer. The answer checker asks for the number before it.

examples.title: Give the same value as a percentage
examples.question: Convert \(\frac{37}{100}\). Give the percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.
solution: Divide the numerator by the denominator to give \(0.37\).
Multiply that decimal by \(100\). The fraction equals \(37\%\).

examples.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
examples.question: Write \(117\%\) as an exact decimal.
solution: Percent means per hundred. First write the value as \(\frac{117}{100}\).
Dividing by \(100\) gives \(1.17\).

examples.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
examples.question: Write \(0.054\) as a percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.
solution: One whole is \(100\%\). Multiply the decimal value by \(100\).

examples.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
examples.question: Write \(6.5\%\) as an exact decimal.
solution: Percent means per hundred. First write the value as \(\frac{6.5}{100}\).
Dividing by \(100\) gives \(0.065\).

examples.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
examples.question: Write \(138\%\) as an exact decimal.
solution: Percent means per hundred. First write the value as \(\frac{138}{100}\).
Dividing by \(100\) gives \(1.38\).

examples.title: Use a fraction with denominator one hundred
examples.question: Write \(5.5\%\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
solution: The percent sign means per hundred, giving \(\frac{5.5}{100}\).
Remove the decimal in the numerator, if present, by scaling both parts by the same power of ten. Then simplify to \(\frac{11}{200}\).

examples.title: Match the fraction, decimal and percentage
examples.question: Which pair gives the same value as \(\frac{23}{80}\) in both columns?
solution: Its percentage number is \(0.2875\times100=28.75\), so select \(0.2875\), \(28.75\%\).

glossary.definition: A fraction, decimal and percentage with exactly the same value.

extraPractice.title: Give the same value as a percentage
extraPractice.prompt: Convert \(\frac{27}{16}\). Give the decimal value and the percentage number.

retry.feedback: This is the decimal value. Give the number obtained after multiplying it by 100.

extraPractice.hint: The fraction itself is the starting decimal value. Multiply that value by 100 for the percentage.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide the numerator by the denominator to give \(1.6875\).

Multiply that decimal by \(100\). The fraction equals \(168.75\%\).

extraPractice.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(236\%\) as an exact decimal.

retry.feedback: Percent means per hundred. Divide the given percentage number by 100.

extraPractice.hint: Anchor the conversion with 1 = 100 per cent.
extraPractice.solution:
Percent means per hundred. First write the value as \(\frac{236}{100}\).

Dividing by \(100\) gives \(2.36\).

extraPractice.title: Convert between the decimal and percentage
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(0.037\) as a percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.

retry.feedback: The field asks for the percentage number. Multiply the decimal by 100.

extraPractice.hint: Anchor the conversion with 1 = 100 per cent.
extraPractice.solution:
One whole is \(100\%\). Multiply the decimal value by \(100\).

\(0.037\times100=3.7\) gives \(3.7\%\).

extraPractice.title: Use a fraction with denominator one hundred
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(109.5\%\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
extraPractice.hint: The percent sign becomes “over 100” before you work with the fraction.
extraPractice.solution:
The percent sign means per hundred, giving \(\frac{109.5}{100}\).

Remove the decimal in the numerator, if present, by scaling both parts by the same power of ten. Then simplify to \(\frac{219}{200}\).

extraPractice.title: Give the same value as a percentage
extraPractice.prompt: Convert \(\frac{17}{125}\). Give the decimal value and the percentage number.

retry.feedback: This is the decimal value. Give the number obtained after multiplying it by 100.

extraPractice.hint: The fraction itself is the starting decimal value. Multiply that value by 100 for the percentage.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide the numerator by the denominator to give \(0.136\).

Multiply that decimal by \(100\). The fraction equals \(13.6\%\).

extraPractice.title: Match the fraction, decimal and percentage
extraPractice.prompt: Which pair gives the same value as \(\frac{43}{200}\) in both columns?
extraPractice.hint: The correct pair must match the fraction in both entries.

revision.body:
Conversion methods

Starting pointWhat to do
Meaning\(p\%=\tfrac p{100}\)
Decimal → percentageMultiply by \(100\) and attach \(\%\).
Percentage → decimalDivide the percentage number by \(100\).
Percentage → simplest fractionPut the number over 100, clear decimals and reduce.
revision.checks:
• Decide which direction uses multiplication.
  • One whole is \(100\%\).
  • Check both entries when matching forms.
revision.examTip: Write the percent sign in written work. A missing percent sign leaves a different number.

igcse-0580-fdp-recurring.description: Extended E1.4. Read recurring notation, use the cycle of remainders and convert exactly between recurring decimals and fractions.

sections.title: Which digits recur?
sections.label: Read bars and dots
sections.intro: Extended only (E1.4). A decimal can have digits before its repeating block.

blocks.html: A bar covers the full block. One dot marks a single repeated digit. Two dots mark the first and last digits of a longer block.
Putting a mark over a digit before the block changes the value.

blocks.title: Mark exactly the repeating block
blocks.prompt: Choose the correct bar notation for \(0.2565656\ldots\). The displayed block continues in the same pattern.
blocks.hint: Write two full copies of the block and check which digits occur before those copies.
blocks.solution:
The digits \(2\) come before the block and do not repeat.

The complete block is \(56\). A bar belongs above every digit in that block, giving \(0.2\overline{56}\).

blocks.html: Read at least two matching copies of the block before writing the shorthand.

sections.title: Why do powers of ten help?
sections.label: Align a repeat
sections.intro: Multiplying by 10 shifts everything one place, including the repeating block.

blocks.html: If the repeat begins immediately, multiply by \(10^n\) for an \(n\)-digit block. The repeating tails line up.
Multiplying by 10 may not line up a repeating block of several digits.

blocks.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
blocks.prompt: Write \(0.\dot{6}\dot{2}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
blocks.hint: First move past the digits that do not recur. Then move one complete repeating block further.
blocks.solution:
The non-recurring block has \(0\) digits and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=0.\dot{6}\dot{2}\).

Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(100x\)\(62.\overline{62}\)
\(1x\)\(0.\overline{62}\)

Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(99x=62\).

Divide by \(99\) and simplify to \(\frac{62}{99}\).

blocks.html: Write your two equations one above the other so the decimal points and repeated blocks can be compared.

sections.title: How does a non-recurring prefix change the equation?
sections.label: Shift past the prefix
sections.intro: Some digits can occur once before the repeated part starts. Use two powers of ten.

blocks.html: If \(m\) non-recurring digits come first and \(n\) digits repeat, use \(10^{m+n}x\) and \(10^mx\). Subtract when the tails match.
The prefix length and the block length do different jobs. Keep zeros inside a block when counting its length.

blocks.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
blocks.prompt: Write \(0.3\dot{1}\dot{6}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
blocks.hint: First move past the digits that do not recur. Then move one complete repeating block further.
blocks.solution:
The non-recurring block has \(1\) digit and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=0.3\dot{1}\dot{6}\).

Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(1000x\)\(316.\overline{16}\)
\(10x\)\(3.\overline{16}\)

Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(990x=313\).

Divide by \(990\) and simplify to \(\frac{313}{990}\).

blocks.html: Check the two tails are identical before subtracting and simplifying.

sections.title: How does long division tell you precisely what repeats?
sections.label: Mark the remainder cycle
sections.intro: Each new digit comes from multiplying the current remainder by ten and dividing by the denominator.

blocks.html: A zero remainder stops the decimal. When the same non-zero remainder comes back, the subsequent digits repeat.

figure.alt: Six numbered circles form a clockwise loop, with successive remainders one, three, two, six, four and five, returning to one.
figure.caption: These are the remainders when dividing \(\frac{1}{7}\) using decimal places. Returning to remainder \(1\) restarts the entire quotient block \(142857\).

blocks.html: Stopping at the first repeated digit may give the wrong block. Check the remainder.

blocks.title: Find the recurring block from remainders
blocks.prompt: Which exact decimal equals \(\frac{2}{27}\)? The bar marks the whole repeating block.
blocks.hint: When the same remainder returns, the same digits start to appear again.
blocks.solution:
Divide the numerator by the denominator. Write the quotient digits in order.

Remainder inNext digitRemainder out
\(2\)\(0\)\(20\)
\(20\)\(7\)\(11\)
\(11\)\(4\)\(2\)

The first repeated remainder restarts the same sequence of digits. \(0.074074\ldots\) therefore equals \(0.\dot{0}7\dot{4}\) or \(0.\overline{074}\).

blocks.html: Include a leading zero if it is part of the recurring block.

sections.title: What can the reduced denominator tell you?
sections.label: Check the reduced fraction
sections.intro: A terminating decimal can be written as a fraction whose denominator is a power of ten.

blocks.html: In simplest form, a denominator with no prime factors apart from 2 and 5 divides a power of ten. The other denominators give a recurring decimal.
Use the reduced denominator. Cancelling a factor can change which prime factors remain.

blocks.title: Decide whether the exact decimal stops
blocks.prompt: Will the decimal expansion of \(\frac{5}{18}\) terminate or recur?
blocks.hint: A denominator with no prime factors other than 2 and 5 gives a terminating decimal.
blocks.solution:
Simplify to \(\frac{5}{18}\). Only the reduced denominator determines what happens.

A power of ten has only prime factors \(2,\ 5\). The reduced denominator also has a prime factor other than 2 and 5.

The exact expansion is \(0.2\overline{7}\).

blocks.html: Long division is a second check when you are unsure whether the decimal stops.

examples.title: Mark exactly the repeating block
examples.question: Write \(0.1646464\ldots\) using a bar over the shortest repeating block.
solution: The digit \(1\) comes before the repeating block.
The complete block is \(64\). A bar belongs above every digit in that block, giving \(0.1\overline{64}\).

examples.title: Mark exactly the repeating block
examples.question: Write \(2.071071071\ldots\) using a bar over the shortest repeating block.
solution: The repetition begins immediately after the decimal point.
The complete block is \(071\). A bar belongs above every digit in that block, giving \(2.\overline{071}\).

examples.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
examples.question: Write \(0.\overline{48}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
solution: The non-recurring block has \(0\) digits and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=0.\overline{48}\).
Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(100x\)\(48.\overline{48}\)
\(x\)\(0.\overline{48}\)
Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(99x=48\).
Divide by \(99\) and simplify to \(\frac{16}{33}\).

examples.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
examples.question: Write \(1.3\dot{7}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
solution: The non-recurring block has \(1\) digit and the recurring block has \(1\) digit. Let \(x=1.3\dot{7}\).
Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(100x\)\(137.\overline{7}\)
\(10x\)\(13.\overline{7}\)
Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(90x=124\).
Divide by \(90\) and simplify to \(\frac{62}{45}\).

examples.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
examples.question: Write \(0.05\overline{24}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
solution: The non-recurring block has \(2\) digits and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=0.05\overline{24}\).
Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(10000x\)\(524.\overline{24}\)
\(100x\)\(5.\overline{24}\)
Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(9900x=519\).
Divide by \(9900\) and simplify to \(\frac{173}{3300}\).

examples.title: Find the recurring block from remainders
examples.question: Which exact decimal equals \(\frac{1}{7}\)? The bar marks the whole repeating block.
solution: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Write the quotient digits in order.

Remainder inNext digitRemainder out
\(1\)\(1\)\(3\)
\(3\)\(4\)\(2\)
\(2\)\(2\)\(6\)
\(6\)\(8\)\(4\)
\(4\)\(5\)\(5\)
\(5\)\(7\)\(1\)
The first repeated remainder restarts the same sequence of digits. \(0.142857142857\ldots\) therefore equals \(0.\dot{1}4285\dot{7}\) or \(0.\overline{142857}\).

examples.title: Decide whether the exact decimal stops
examples.question: Will the decimal expansion of \(\frac{27}{72}\) terminate or recur?
solution: Simplify to \(\frac{3}{8}\). Only the reduced denominator determines what happens.
A power of ten has only prime factors \(2,\ 5\). The reduced denominator divides a power of ten.
The exact expansion is \(0.375\).

glossary.definition: A decimal whose digits repeat a block indefinitely.
The shortest group of digits that repeats without a break.
The digits after the decimal point which occur before the repeat begins.
What is left after one division step. The next digit depends on it.

extraPractice.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(1.0\overline{52}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
extraPractice.hint: First move past the digits that do not recur. Then move one complete repeating block further.
extraPractice.solution:
The non-recurring block has \(1\) digit and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=1.0\overline{52}\).

ExpressionValue

\(10x\)\(10.\overline{52}\)

Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(990x=1042\).

Divide by \(990\) and simplify to \(\frac{521}{495}\).

Remainder inNext digitRemainder out

The first repeated remainder restarts the same sequence of digits. \(0.3611\ldots\) therefore equals \(0.36\dot{1}\) or \(0.36\overline{1}\).

extraPractice.title: Mark exactly the repeating block
extraPractice.prompt: Choose the correct bar notation for \(0.4727272\ldots\). The displayed block continues in the same pattern.
extraPractice.hint: Write two full copies of the block and check which digits occur before those copies.
extraPractice.solution:
The digits \(4\) come before the block and do not repeat.

The complete block is \(72\). A bar belongs above every digit in that block, giving \(0.4\overline{72}\).

extraPractice.title: Line up the repeat before subtracting
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(0.03\dot{8}\dot{1}\) as a fraction in simplest form. Give the numerator and denominator.
extraPractice.hint: First move past the digits that do not recur. Then move one complete repeating block further.
extraPractice.solution:
The non-recurring block has \(2\) digits and the recurring block has \(2\) digits. Let \(x=0.03\dot{8}\dot{1}\).

Shift the two numbers so the same block starts immediately after the decimal point in both rows.

ExpressionValue
\(10000x\)\(381.\overline{81}\)
\(100x\)\(3.\overline{81}\)

Subtract the lower row from the upper row. The repeating part cancels, giving \(9900x=378\).

Divide by \(9900\) and simplify to \(\frac{21}{550}\).

extraPractice.title: Find the recurring block from remainders
extraPractice.prompt: Which exact decimal equals \(\frac{29}{33}\)? The bar marks the whole repeating block.
extraPractice.hint: When the same remainder returns, the same digits start to appear again.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide the numerator by the denominator. Write the quotient digits in order.

Remainder inNext digitRemainder out
\(29\)\(8\)\(26\)
\(26\)\(7\)\(29\)

The first repeated remainder restarts the same sequence of digits. \(0.8787\ldots\) therefore equals \(0.\dot{8}\dot{7}\) or \(0.\overline{87}\).

extraPractice.title: Decide whether the exact decimal stops
extraPractice.prompt: Will the decimal expansion of \(\frac{18}{45}\) terminate or recur?
extraPractice.hint: A denominator with no prime factors other than 2 and 5 gives a terminating decimal.
extraPractice.solution:
Simplify to \(\frac{2}{5}\). Only the reduced denominator determines what happens.

A power of ten has only prime factors \(2,\ 5\). The reduced denominator divides a power of ten.

The exact expansion is \(0.4\).

revision.body:
Conversion methods

Starting pointWhat to do
Read the notationBar above a block, or dots above its first and last digits.
Fraction → recurring decimalDivide until a non-zero remainder returns.
Recurring decimal → fractionUse two powers of ten to align the repeated tails, then subtract.
Terminating testReduce first. Only prime factors 2 and 5 may remain in the denominator.
revision.checks:
• Read the whole prefix before marking the repeat.
  • Keep zeros which belong to the repeated block.
  • Simplify the final fraction.
revision.examTip: Use several written decimal places to show that the recurring tails line up. A rounded calculator value cannot establish an exact fraction.
